Kinsmen
KINZ-men
n. pl.
From kin, Saxon cynn, race or family, and men. Webster 1828: relatives; those of the same blood or family. In the Old Testament the kinsman carries a legal office — the goel, the redeemer of a relative’s person, land, and blood.

Biblical Definition

Kinsmen are blood relatives, and in Israel the relation carried duties that no other society imposed. The nearest kinsman was obliged to redeem a relative sold into servitude, to buy back land the family had lost, to avenge shed blood, and in some cases to raise up seed to a dead brother — the whole office of the goel, which is the machinery of the book of Ruth and the type behind the doctrine of redemption. Paul writes with anguish about his own kinsmen: For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3) — the strongest expression of love for an unbelieving people in Scripture. He greets kinsmen among the Roman Christians: Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me (Romans 16:7). And the Lord uses kinsmen to overturn the ordinary logic of hospitality: When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee (Luke 14:12) — invite instead those who cannot repay.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KINSMAN as a man of the same race or family; one related by blood; and in the plural, relatives or kindred. The Hebrew law attached particular obligations of redemption to the nearest kinsman.

KINSMEN, n. pl. of KINSMAN — Men of the same race or family; relatives by blood.

KINSMAN, n. — A man of the same kin or family; a relative.

In Hebrew law, the near kinsman had the right and duty of redeeming a relative’s person or inheritance.

KIN, n. — Relation, properly by consanguinity or descent from a common ancestor.

From Saxon cynn, kind, race, family — the root also of kind, kindred, and king.

Key Scripture

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:"

Romans 16:7 — "Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me."

Luke 14:12 — "Then said he also to him that bade him, When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee."

Leviticus 25:49 — "Either his uncle, or his uncle's son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself."

Modern Corruption

Romans 16:7 is regularly produced as proof that a woman held apostolic office, which requires both a disputed reading of the name and a disputed sense of a phrase, and cannot bear the weight placed on it against the plain teaching of 1 Timothy 2.

expand to see more

Two questions are involved and neither is settled in the way egalitarian readings require. The first is whether the name is Junia, a woman, or Junias, a man; the Authorized Version prints Junia, and the dictionary sees no need to dispute it. The second is what of note among the apostles means, and here the Greek can equally mean well known to the apostles rather than numbered among them — a reading held by Chrysostom’s critics and by many since. Even granting the inclusive sense, apostle in the New Testament often means a sent messenger of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25) rather than one of the Twelve. A single greeting in a list of salutations cannot overturn 1 Timothy 2:12 and 1 Timothy 3:1-7, which state the rule directly and give the reason from the creation order.

What Romans 9:3 shows is more worth dwelling on and is almost never preached. Paul, who had been stoned, beaten and hounded by his own countrymen, says he could wish himself accursed from Christ for their sake — the strongest thing a man could say, and only Moses in Exodus 32:32 says anything comparable. That is what love for the lost sounds like in an apostle, and it is stated about the very people who wanted him dead. Luke 14:12 gives the practical outworking for ordinary households: the Lord tells a host not to invite those who can repay him. Hospitality aimed at people who cannot return it is one of the few Christian practices whose motive cannot be mistaken.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew goel (H1350 participle), a kinsman-redeemer; gaal (H1350), to redeem, to act as kinsman; qarob (H7138), near, a near relative; Greek suggenes (G4773), a kinsman.

expand to see more

Hebrew goel — the kinsman-redeemer; the office Boaz fulfils in Ruth 4 and the type behind Christ’s redemption.

Hebrew gaal (H1350) — to redeem, to buy back as a kinsman; I know that my redeemer liveth (Job 19:25).

Hebrew qarob (H7138) — near, a near kinsman; any that is nigh of kin unto him (Leviticus 25:49).

Greek suggenes (G4773) — a relative, one of the same stock; my kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3).

Greek lutrotes (G3086) — a redeemer, a ransomer; the New Testament term for the office Christ fills (Acts 7:35).

Usage

"My kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3) — a man willing to be accursed for the people who hunted him."

"Call not… thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours (Luke 14:12) — hospitality aimed where it cannot be repaid."

"Any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him (Leviticus 25:49) — the office of the kinsman-redeemer."
